title: Chapter 3: Tripura — British Period, Partition, and Merger with India

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: During British rule, Tripura was recognized as a princely state known as Hill Tipperah, retaining internal administrative autonomy.
The 1947 Partition of India cut off Tripura's mainland routes and detached Chakla Roshnabad, creating severe economic and geographical isolation.
Regent Maharani Kanchan Prabha Devi signed the Tripura Merger Agreement on October 9, 1949, on behalf of minor Maharaja Kirit Bikram Kishore Manikya.
Tripura officially integrated into India on October 15, 1949, transitioning through Part C State and Union Territory statuses before gaining full statehood in 1972.
Large-scale refugee influxes from East Pakistan fundamentally altered the demographic composition, leading to socio-economic friction and political insurgency.

blocks.content: Unlike most princely states, Tripura maintained a semi-independent status throughout British rule. The British East India Company and later the Crown recognised Tripura's internal sovereignty while exercising paramountcy over external affairs. The Manikya kings signed a 'Subsidiary Alliance' type arrangement with the British, remaining autonomous in internal governance.

items: 1808: First formal treaty between Tripura and British East India Company
British Political Agent: A British Resident was stationed at Agartala to oversee relations
Partition of Bengal (1905): Tripura briefly found itself near the new borders of Eastern Bengal
Agitprop movements: The Bengali intelligentsia of Tripura participated in freedom movements; Tripura Congress was established
The Manikya kings generally supported the British during World Wars I and II, contributing troops and resources
Tripura State Committee (Praja Mandal): Peasant and tribal rights movement in the 1930s-40s; demanded responsible government from the Manikya kings

blocks.content: Tripura officially merged with the Indian Union on October 15, 1949.

The partition of British India in 1947 was catastrophic for Tripura in ways unique to this state. The creation of Pakistan (East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) effectively surrounded Tripura on three sides. The consequences were profound and long-lasting:

rows: Part C State (1949), UT (1956), Full State (1972)
Included Hill Tipperah and Chakla Roshnabad estate
Confined to hilly boundaries; Chakla Roshnabad lost to East Pakistan
Demographic shift due to refugee influx from East Pakistan

items: Demographic transformation: Millions of Hindu Bengali refugees from East Pakistan flooded into Tripura between 1947 and 1971 — changing Tripura from a tribal-majority to a Bengali-majority state
Before 1947: Tribal population was about 50% of Tripura; after large-scale refugee influx, it fell to about 28-31%
Economic disruption: Trade routes, which ran through East Pakistan territory, were disrupted; Tripura became economically isolated
Cultural impact: Bengali culture became dominant; the tribal communities felt marginalised — leading to ethnic tensions and insurgency later
1947-1971: First wave of refugees; millions from East Pakistan's Hindu minority settled in Tripura
1971 Bangladesh Liberation War: Another wave — first refugees fleeing Pakistani atrocities, then some returning after Bangladesh independence
Post-1971 illegal immigration: Continued, mostly Muslim Bangladeshis; changed demographics of some areas

blocks.content: After India's independence in 1947, the princely states were required to accede to either India or Pakistan. Tripura, being a Hindu-majority state surrounded by the new East Pakistan, naturally joined India. The merger process:

items: Maharani Kanchan Prabha Devi served as Regent and signed the Tripura Merger Agreement on October 9, 1949.
Chakla Roshnabad was the fertile plain zamindari estate of Tripura's kings that was allocated to East Pakistan during Partition.
Tripura attained full statehood under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act on January 21, 1972.
October 15, 1947: Tripura acceded to India (Instrument of Accession signed)
9 September 1949: Full merger agreement signed — Tripura became a Part C State of India under a Chief Commissioner
Last Maharaja: Kirit Bikram Kishore Manikya signed the merger; he was the last ruling Manikya king
The Maharani (Queen) was given a privy purse, as with other princely states, until 1971 when privy purses were abolished by Indira Gandhi
1956: Tripura reorganised as a Union Territory under the States Reorganisation Act
21 January 1972: Tripura became a full-fledged state of India (along with Manipur and Meghalaya) — celebrated as Tripura Statehood Day

blocks.content: 3.4 Refugees, Insurgency, and Political History Post-Merger

cells: Tripura merged as Part C State under a Chief Commissioner
Indian National Congress (INC) wins; Sachindra Lal Singh becomes first Chief Minister
Under States Reorganisation Act; still administered by Centre
Tripura, Manipur and Meghalaya become full states
CPI(M)-led Left Front wins; begins 25-year dominance of Tripura politics
Tribal groups demanding autonomy; ethnic conflict between tribal and Bengali settlers; TUJS (Tripura Upajati Juba Samiti), TNV (Tripura National Volunteers) armed movements
Constitutional body under 6th Schedule to protect tribal rights in 68.1% of Tripura's geographical area; a key peace measure
Left Front ruled Tripura for 25 of 27 years; Manik Sarkar became iconic long-serving CM (1998–2018)
Longest-serving CM (20 years); known for personal simplicity and anti-corruption; Tripura's literacy reached 88%
BJP-IPFT alliance wins 43 of 60 seats; ends Left Front's 25-year rule; Biplab Kumar Deb becomes CM
BJP's first CM; controversial statements made him famous; development focus
Biplab Kumar Deb resigned; Manik Saha (dentist-turned-politician) became CM; 2023 election returned BJP to power
BJP wins 32 seats (reduced from 43); Manik Saha continues as CM; TIPRA Motha (new tribal party under Pradyot Kishore Manikya) wins 13 seats
